claim: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) affects myofibers and muscle stem cells, causing progressive muscle degeneration and repair defects.
source: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) affects myofibers and muscle stem cells, causing progressive muscle degeneration and repair defects.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract summarizing established knowledge about DMD pathology.

claim: In Dmdmdx myoblasts lacking full-length dystrophin, the expression of 170 genes was significantly altered.
source: In Dmdmdx myoblasts lacking full-length dystrophin, the expression of 170 genes was significantly altered.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq differential expression analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Myod1 and key genes controlled by MyoD (Myog, Mymk, Mymx, epigenetic regulators, ECM interactors, calcium signalling and fibrosis genes) were significantly downregulated in Dmdmdx myoblasts.
source: Myod1 and key genes controlled by MyoD (Myog, Mymk, Mymx, epigenetic regulators, ECM interactors, calcium signalling and fibrosis genes) were significantly downregulated.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data and qPCR validation shown in the results.

claim: Gene ontology analysis indicated enrichment in genes involved in muscle development and function in dystrophic myoblasts.
source: Gene ontology analysis indicated enrichment in genes involved in muscle development and function.
evidence: GO enrichment analysis was performed on differentially expressed genes.

claim: Dystrophic myoblasts show increased proliferation compared to wild-type controls.
source: Functionally, we found increased myoblast proliferation, reduced chemotaxis and accelerated differentiation, which are all essential for myoregeneration.
evidence: BrDU incorporation assays demonstrated increased proliferation in dystrophic myoblasts.

claim: Dystrophic myoblasts show reduced chemotaxis compared to wild-type controls.
source: Functionally, we found increased myoblast proliferation, reduced chemotaxis and accelerated differentiation, which are all essential for myoregeneration.
evidence: Boyden chamber assays demonstrated reduced chemotaxis in dystrophic myoblasts.

claim: Dystrophic myoblasts show accelerated differentiation compared to wild-type controls.
source: Functionally, we found increased myoblast proliferation, reduced chemotaxis and accelerated differentiation, which are all essential for myoregeneration.
evidence: 3D spheroid differentiation assays with qPCR analysis of differentiation markers demonstrated accelerated differentiation.

claim: The defects in dystrophic myoblasts were caused by the loss of expression of full-length dystrophin, as similar and not exacerbated alterations were observed in dystrophin-null Dmdmdx-βgeo myoblasts.
source: The defects were caused by the loss of expression of full-length dystrophin, as similar and not exacerbated alterations were observed in dystrophin-null Dmdmdx-βgeo myoblasts.
evidence: Comparison of Dmdmdx and Dmdmdx-βgeo transcriptomes showed similar alterations without exacerbation.

claim: Corresponding abnormalities were identified in human DMD primary myoblasts, confirming the cross-species nature of these defects.
source: Corresponding abnormalities were identified in human DMD primary myoblasts and a dystrophic mouse muscle cell line, confirming the cross-species and cell-autonomous nature of these defects.
evidence: RNA-Seq analysis of human DMD myoblasts showed similar transcriptomic alterations and GO enrichment patterns as mouse dystrophic myoblasts.

claim: Corresponding abnormalities were identified in a dystrophic mouse muscle cell line, confirming the cell-autonomous nature of these defects.
source: Corresponding abnormalities were identified in human DMD primary myoblasts and a dystrophic mouse muscle cell line, confirming the cross-species and cell-autonomous nature of these defects.
evidence: SC5 dystrophic cell line showed similar transcriptomic and functional alterations as primary dystrophic myoblasts.

claim: The genome-scale metabolic analysis in human DMD myoblasts showed alterations in the rate of glycolysis/gluconeogenesis.
source: The genome-scale metabolic analysis in human DMD myoblasts showed alterations in the rate of glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, leukotriene metabolism, and mitochondrial beta-oxidation of various fatty acids.
evidence: Enzyme-constrained genome-scale metabolic modeling using RNA-Seq data identified altered metabolic pathways.

claim: The genome-scale metabolic analysis in human DMD myoblasts showed alterations in leukotriene metabolism.
source: The genome-scale metabolic analysis in human DMD myoblasts showed alterations in the rate of glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, leukotriene metabolism, and mitochondrial beta-oxidation of various fatty acids.
evidence: Enzyme-constrained genome-scale metabolic modeling using RNA-Seq data identified altered metabolic pathways.

claim: The genome-scale metabolic analysis in human DMD myoblasts showed alterations in mitochondrial beta-oxidation of various fatty acids.
source: The genome-scale metabolic analysis in human DMD myoblasts showed alterations in the rate of glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, leukotriene metabolism, and mitochondrial beta-oxidation of various fatty acids.
evidence: Enzyme-constrained genome-scale metabolic modeling using RNA-Seq data identified altered metabolic pathways.

claim: DMD is caused by mutations in the DMD gene located on the X chromosome.
source: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a debilitating and lethal neuromuscular disorder caused by mutations in the DMD gene located on the X chromosome (Hoffman et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Hoffman et al., 1988.

claim: DMD diagnosis is made between the age of 2 and 5.
source: Diagnosis is made between the age of 2 and 5, loss of ambulation occurs around 12 and young adults die due to respiratory and/or cardiac failure (Koeks et al., 2017).
evidence: This clinical information is supported by citation to Koeks et al., 2017.

claim: Loss of ambulation in DMD occurs around age 12.
source: Diagnosis is made between the age of 2 and 5, loss of ambulation occurs around 12 and young adults die due to respiratory and/or cardiac failure (Koeks et al., 2017).
evidence: This clinical information is supported by citation to Koeks et al., 2017.

claim: Young adults with DMD die due to respiratory and/or cardiac failure.
source: Diagnosis is made between the age of 2 and 5, loss of ambulation occurs around 12 and young adults die due to respiratory and/or cardiac failure (Koeks et al., 2017).
evidence: This clinical information is supported by citation to Koeks et al., 2017.

claim: DMD is the largest human gene known.
source: DMD is the largest human gene known (Tennyson et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tennyson et al., 1995.

claim: Three full-length DMD transcripts encode 427 kDa proteins.
source: Three full-length transcripts encode 427 kDa proteins, while further intragenic promoters drive the expression of progressively truncated variants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DMD gene structure and protein products.

claim: Dp427 and the dystrophin-associated protein complex (DAPC) are important for the functional development of differentiating myotubes.
source: Dp427 and the dystrophin-associated protein complex (DAPC) are important for the functional development of differentiating myotubes (Shoji et al., 2015) and subsequently prevent contraction-induced injury in the mature muscle (Rader et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shoji et al., 2015.

claim: Dp427 and DAPC prevent contraction-induced injury in mature muscle.
source: Dp427 and the dystrophin-associated protein complex (DAPC) are important for the functional development of differentiating myotubes (Shoji et al., 2015) and subsequently prevent contraction-induced injury in the mature muscle (Rader et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rader et al., 2016.

claim: The ablation of dystrophin in fully differentiated myofibres did not trigger their degeneration.
source: Several studies showed that the ablation of dystrophin in fully differentiated myofibres did not trigger their degeneration (Rader et al., 2016; Ghahramani Seno et al., 2008), and even that myofibres can function without dystrophin (Waugh et al., 2014; Vieira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rader et al., 2016 and Ghahramani Seno et al., 2008.

claim: Myofibres can function without dystrophin.
source: Several studies showed that the ablation of dystrophin in fully differentiated myofibres did not trigger their degeneration (Rader et al., 2016; Ghahramani Seno et al., 2008), and even that myofibres can function without dystrophin (Waugh et al., 2014; Vieira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Waugh et al., 2014 and Vieira et al., 2015.

claim: DMD pathology is active prior to diagnosis, with delays in the attainment of motor and non-motor milestones discernible in 2 months old DMD babies.
source: In fact, DMD pathology is active prior to diagnosis: delays in the attainment of motor and non‐motor milestones are discernible in 2 months old DMD babies (van Dommelen et al., 2020) and transcriptomes of muscles from asymptomatic DMD patients revealed typical dystrophic abnormalities (Pescatori et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Dommelen et al., 2020.

claim: Transcriptomes of muscles from asymptomatic DMD patients revealed typical dystrophic abnormalities.
source: In fact, DMD pathology is active prior to diagnosis: delays in the attainment of motor and non‐motor milestones are discernible in 2 months old DMD babies (van Dommelen et al., 2020) and transcriptomes of muscles from asymptomatic DMD patients revealed typical dystrophic abnormalities (Pescatori et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pescatori et al., 2007.

claim: Studies of human foetuses revealed that DMD pathology starts in prenatal development.
source: Studies of human foetuses (Toop and Emery, 1977; Emery, 1977; Vassilopoulos and Emery, 1977) and various animal DMD models, including GRMD dogs (Nguyen et al., 2002), Sapje zebrafish (Bassett et al., 1977) and Dmdmdx mouse embryos (Merrick et al., 2009) revealed that the pathology starts already in prenatal development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Toop and Emery, 1977; Emery, 1977; Vassilopoulos and Emery, 1977.

claim: Various animal DMD models including GRMD dogs, Sapje zebrafish and Dmdmdx mouse embryos revealed that the pathology starts in prenatal development.
source: Studies of human foetuses (Toop and Emery, 1977; Emery, 1977; Vassilopoulos and Emery, 1977) and various animal DMD models, including GRMD dogs (Nguyen et al., 2002), Sapje zebrafish (Bassett et al., 1977) and Dmdmdx mouse embryos (Merrick et al., 2009) revealed that the pathology starts already in prenatal development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nguyen et al., 2002; Bassett et al., 1977; Merrick et al., 2009.

claim: In skeletal muscle lineages modelled in human DMD pluripotent stem cells, marked transcriptome and miRNA dysregulations are identifiable even before muscle specialisation.
source: Indeed, in skeletal muscle lineages modelled in human DMD pluripotent stem cells, we have recently demonstrated marked transcriptome and miRNA dysregulations identifiable even before muscle specialisation (Mournetas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mournetas et al., 2021.

claim: The specific embryonic dystrophin Dp412e exists.
source: These data, combined with the existence of the specific embryonic dystrophin Dp412e (Massouridès et al., 2015), substantiate the early disease manifestations in muscle precursor cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Massouridès et al., 2015.

claim: There is increasing evidence that dysregulation of myogenic cells is behind muscle pathology and disease progression in adult DMD muscle.
source: Importantly, there is increasing evidence that dysregulation of myogenic cells is behind muscle pathology and disease progression in adult DMD muscle.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on accumulating evidence in the field.

claim: Helen Blau proposed that DMD is intrinsic to the undifferentiated myoblast.
source: Helen Blau proposed that DMD is intrinsic to the undifferentiated myoblast (Blau et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blau et al., 1983.

claim: The hypothesis that DMD is intrinsic to the undifferentiated myoblast was initially discounted.
source: This hypothesis was initially discounted (Hurko et al., 1987), but there is new evidence that DMD mutations produce a range of cell-autonomous abnormalities in both human and mouse myogenic cells from adult muscles (Yablonka-Reuveni and Anderson, 2006; Yeung et al., 2006; Sacco et al., 2010; Górecki, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hurko et al., 1987.

claim: There is new evidence that DMD mutations produce a range of cell-autonomous abnormalities in both human and mouse myogenic cells from adult muscles.
source: This hypothesis was initially discounted (Hurko et al., 1987), but there is new evidence that DMD mutations produce a range of cell-autonomous abnormalities in both human and mouse myogenic cells from adult muscles (Yablonka-Reuveni and Anderson, 2006; Yeung et al., 2006; Sacco et al., 2010; Górecki, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yablonka-Reuveni and Anderson, 2006; Yeung et al., 2006; Sacco et al., 2010; Górecki, 2016.

claim: The Dmdmdx mouse has a stop codon mutation in exon 23.
source: The Dmdmdx has a stop codon mutation in exon 23 (Sicinski et al., 1989) resulting in the loss of full-length (Dp427) dystrophin expression, which reflects the molecular defect affecting the majority of DMD patients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sicinski et al., 1989.

claim: The Dmdmdx mutation results in the loss of full-length (Dp427) dystrophin expression.
source: The Dmdmdx has a stop codon mutation in exon 23 (Sicinski et al., 1989) resulting in the loss of full-length (Dp427) dystrophin expression, which reflects the molecular defect affecting the majority of DMD patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Dmdmdx mouse model.

claim: The Dmdmdx molecular defect reflects the molecular defect affecting the majority of DMD patients.
source: The Dmdmdx has a stop codon mutation in exon 23 (Sicinski et al., 1989) resulting in the loss of full-length (Dp427) dystrophin expression, which reflects the molecular defect affecting the majority of DMD patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relevance of the Dmdmdx model to human DMD.

claim: The clinical phenotype in 3–10 weeks old Dmdmdx is as aggressive as in Duchenne patients.
source: Detailed histological and molecular analyses indicated that the clinical phenotype in 3–10 weeks old Dmdmdx is as aggressive as in Duchenne patients (Duddy et al., 2015; DiMario et al., 1991; Massopust et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duddy et al., 2015; DiMario et al., 1991; Massopust et al., 2020.

claim: After the phase of severe degeneration-regeneration, most Dmdmdx muscles start to regenerate due to an unknown mechanism.
source: Therefore, during this period, Dmdmdx is a good model for the human pathology. Unlike human, after this phase of severe degeneration-regeneration, most Dmdmdx muscles start to regenerate (DiMario et al., 1991) due to an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by citation to DiMario et al., 1991, with the mechanism noted as unknown.

claim: Dp427 is expressed in satellite cells and myofibres.
source: While Dp427 is expressed in satellite cells and myofibres and its loss in Dmdmdx reflects the predominant molecular defect in DMD patients, dystrophin Dp71 is present in regenerating muscles and specifically in myoblasts (Howard et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about dystrophin expression patterns.

claim: Dystrophin Dp71 is present in regenerating muscles and specifically in myoblasts.
source: While Dp427 is expressed in satellite cells and myofibres and its loss in Dmdmdx reflects the predominant molecular defect in DMD patients, dystrophin Dp71 is present in regenerating muscles and specifically in myoblasts (Howard et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Howard et al., 1999.

claim: Dmdmdx-βgeo mice lack all dystrophins.
source: Given that we have recently described exacerbated pathology in Dmdmdx-βgeo mice lacking all dystrophins (Young et al., 2020), we also investigated the consequences of the total loss of Dmd expression in Dmdmdx-βgeo myoblasts (Wertz and Füchtbauer, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wertz and Füchtbauer, 1998.

claim: Dmdmdx-βgeo mice show exacerbated pathology compared to Dmdmdx mice.
source: Given that we have recently described exacerbated pathology in Dmdmdx-βgeo mice lacking all dystrophins (Young et al., 2020), we also investigated the consequences of the total loss of Dmd expression in Dmdmdx-βgeo myoblasts (Wertz and Füchtbauer, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Young et al., 2020.

claim: Skeletal muscle accounts for around 90% of total oxygen uptake.
source: Given that skeletal muscle is a key metabolic site, accounting for around 90% of total oxygen uptake, muscle metabolism is a significant variable (Zurlo et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zurlo et al., 1990.

claim: Metabolic dysfunction can impair muscle regeneration.
source: Moreover, metabolic dysfunction can impair muscle regeneration, and the impact of DMD on cellular energetics in muscle progenitors has recently been identified (Matre et al., 2019).
evidence: This is general knowledge about muscle biology.

claim: The impact of DMD on cellular energetics in muscle progenitors has recently been identified.
source: Moreover, metabolic dysfunction can impair muscle regeneration, and the impact of DMD on cellular energetics in muscle progenitors has recently been identified (Matre et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Matre et al., 2019.

claim: Sample-based hierarchical clustering clearly segregates genes into two groups corresponding to genotypes (Dmdmdx vs WT).
source: Bioinformatic analysis of the RNA-Seq data showed the impact of the Dmdmdx allele on the primary myoblast transcriptome. Sample-based hierarchical clustering clearly segregates genes into two groups corresponding to genotypes (Figure 1a) and a volcano plot illustrates the presence of a substantial number of significantly dysregulated genes (Figure 1b, Supplementary file 1-1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 1a showing hierarchical clustering of samples.

claim: A volcano plot illustrates the presence of a substantial number of significantly dysregulated genes in Dmdmdx vs WT myoblasts.
source: Bioinformatic analysis of the RNA-Seq data showed the impact of the Dmdmdx allele on the primary myoblast transcriptome. Sample-based hierarchical clustering clearly segregates genes into two groups corresponding to genotypes (Figure 1a) and a volcano plot illustrates the presence of a substantial number of significantly dysregulated genes (Figure 1b, Supplementary file 1-1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 1b showing a volcano plot of differential gene expression.

claim: Myod1 and Myog downregulation in dystrophic myoblasts was confirmed by qPCR.
source: Among these, Myod1 and Myog, key coordinators of skeletal muscle development and repair, were found to be downregulated in dystrophic myoblasts and their downregulation was confirmed by qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qPCR validation data is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pax3 levels were confirmed as significantly downregulated by qPCR in dystrophic myoblasts.
source: Pax3 and Pax7 transcriptional regulators (Magli et al., 2019) were also individually investigated, with Pax3 levels confirmed as significantly downregulated by qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qPCR validation data is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mymx and Bex1, known to be regulators of muscle repair, are downregulated in dystrophic myoblasts.
source: Our analysis identified downregulation of further important regulators and effectors of the muscle program (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1) such as Mymx and Bex1, known to be regulators of muscle repair (Koo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1c and citation to Koo et al., 2007.

claim: Des, a structural component of myofilaments, was found to be significantly downregulated in dystrophic myoblasts.
source: Des, a structural component of myofilaments, and Itga7, the primary laminin-1 receptor of myoblasts and mature fibres were also found to be significantly downregulated (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Itga7, the primary laminin-1 receptor of myoblasts and mature fibres, was found to be significantly downregulated in dystrophic myoblasts.
source: Des, a structural component of myofilaments, and Itga7, the primary laminin-1 receptor of myoblasts and mature fibres were also found to be significantly downregulated (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The H19 gene is defined as promoting differentiation.
source: The H19 gene, defined as promoting differentiation (Qin et al., 2017), was found to be significantly downregulated in proliferating Dmdmdx myoblasts (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1), which combined with reduced expression of aforementioned muscle program markers, as well as myogenic differentiation markers such as Acta1, Actc1, Actn3, Atp2a1 and upregulation of Nov, known to inhibit myogenic differentiation (Sakamoto et al., 2002), imply an altered readiness of dystrophic myoblasts to differentiate.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Qin et al., 2017.

claim: H19 was found to be significantly downregulated in proliferating Dmdmdx myoblasts.
source: The H19 gene, defined as promoting differentiation (Qin et al., 2017), was found to be significantly downregulated in proliferating Dmdmdx myoblasts (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1), which combined with reduced expression of aforementioned muscle program markers, as well as myogenic differentiation markers such as Acta1, Actc1, Actn3, Atp2a1 and upregulation of Nov, known to inhibit myogenic differentiation (Sakamoto et al., 2002), imply an altered readiness of dystrophic myoblasts to differentiate.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Nov is known to inhibit myogenic differentiation.
source: The H19 gene, defined as promoting differentiation (Qin et al., 2017), was found to be significantly downregulated in proliferating Dmdmdx myoblasts (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1), which combined with reduced expression of aforementioned muscle program markers, as well as myogenic differentiation markers such as Acta1, Actc1, Actn3, Atp2a1 and upregulation of Nov, known to inhibit myogenic differentiation (Sakamoto et al., 2002), imply an altered readiness of dystrophic myoblasts to differentiate.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sakamoto et al., 2002.

claim: Numerous genes encoding histones and regulators of chromatin organisation/chromatin interacting proteins were found to be significantly dysregulated in dystrophic myoblasts.
source: Moreover, numerous genes encoding histones and Smyd1 (Li et al., 2009b) and Hmga1 (Harrer et al., 2004; Qiu et al., 2017) regulators of chromatin organisation/chromatin interacting proteins, were found to be significantly dysregulated in dystrophic myoblasts (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1c and citations.

claim: Gene expression changes in dystrophic myoblasts indicated an increased readiness to proliferate, compared to WT counterparts.
source: Taken together, these gene expression changes indicated an increased readiness of dystrophic myoblasts to proliferate, compared to their WT counterparts.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of gene expression changes observed.

claim: Several genes key to myoblast-extracellular matrix interactions and fibrosis were found to be significantly dysregulated in Dmdmdx myoblasts.
source: Several genes key to myoblast-extracellular matrix interactions and fibrosis were found to be significantly dysregulated in Dmdmdx myoblasts (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1), including: Mmp3, Mmp9 and Mmp10 metalloproteases, collagen genes (Col2a1, Col4a1, Col4a2, and Col8a2), Lrrn1 a transmembrane protein interacting with fibronectin (Haines et al., 2005) as well as genes encoding fibronectin itself (Fn1) and decorin (Dcn).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Decorin promotes proliferation and differentiation in myoblasts.
source: The latter promotes proliferation and differentiation in myoblasts (Kishioka et al., 2008) but also has a role in collagen assembly and mineralisation (Mochida et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kishioka et al., 2008.

claim: Decorin has a role in collagen assembly and mineralisation.
source: The latter promotes proliferation and differentiation in myoblasts (Kishioka et al., 2008) but also has a role in collagen assembly and mineralisation (Mochida et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mochida et al., 2009.

claim: Calsequestrins (Casq1 and Casq2) were significantly downregulated in dystrophic myoblasts.
source: Finally, calsequestrins (Casq1 and Casq2) (Supplementary file 1-1) were significantly downregulated, in line with previous observations in the dystrophic muscle (Doran et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data and citation to Doran et al., 2004.

claim: Sample clustering shows no substantial difference between Dmdmdx-βgeo and Dmdmdx myoblast transcriptomes.
source: Corresponding bioinformatic comparison of Dmdmdx-βgeo vs. Dmdmdx myoblast transcriptomes found no substantial difference between them, as illustrated by sample clustering (Figure 2a) and volcano plot (Figure 2b), with no segregation between groups.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 2a showing sample clustering.

claim: Only 11 genes were found to be significantly differentially expressed between Dmdmdx-βgeo and Dmdmdx myoblasts.
source: Only 11 genes were found to be significantly differentially expressed between the two genotypes. Of these, 6 are pseudogenes, 1 is a processed transcript and only 4 are protein-coding genes (Igf1, Npr3, Postn and Capn6).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: A comparison of Dmdmdx-βgeo to WT transcriptome returned fewer (81) significantly differentially expressed genes than Dmdmdx versus WT (170).
source: Interestingly, a comparison of the Dmdmdx-βgeo to the WT transcriptome returned fewer (81) (Supplementary file 1-2) significantly differentially expressed genes than Dmdmdx versus WT (170) (Supplementary file 1-1).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: The two dystrophic models (Dmdmdx and Dmdmdx-βgeo) show strikingly similar alterations with a strong, significant correlation (r=0.9418, p<1.0e-4) in the log2 fold changes.
source: However, a comparison of the fold changes between the two analyses (Figure 2c) revealed that the two models show strikingly similar alterations with a strong, significant correlation (r=0.9418, p<1.0e-4) in the log2 fold changes for genes significantly altered in Dmdmdx versus WT and/or Dmdmdx-βgeo versus WT analyses (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Genes found downregulated in Dmdmdx had increased ChIP-Seq signal at the TFBS for MyoD, TCF12, MYOG, and TCF3.
source: Genes found downregulated in Dmdmdx had increased ChIP-Seq signal at the TFBS for four transcription factors: MyoD (adjusted p-value: 2.9e–21, track GEO accession GSM915165), TCF12 (1e–19, GSM915178), MYOG (5.6e–19, GSM915164), and TCF3 (adjusted p-value 3.3e-3, GSM915177) (Figure 3, Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: A range of genes including Mymk, Mymx, Chrna1, and Acta1 showed a binding signal at their TFBS above the background of at least three out of four overrepresented TFs.
source: A range of genes, including Mymk, Mymx, Chrna1, and Acta1 showed a binding signal at their TFBS above the background of at least three out of four of these overrepresented TFs (Figure 3b, Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Seq data analysis.

claim: Transcripts downregulated in Dmdmdx-βgeo exhibit overrepresentation of MyoD binding sites.
source: Furthermore, transcripts downregulated in Dmdmdx-βgeo also exhibit overrepresentation of MyoD binding sites (Supplementary file 2E).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Seq data analysis.

claim: Genes upregulated in dystrophic myoblasts did not show any statistically significant overrepresentation of the binding signal of any TF.
source: In contrast, genes upregulated in any cell type under investigation did not show any statistically significant overrepresentation of the binding signal of any TF (Supplementary file 2A and D).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Seq data analysis.

claim: GO categories 'muscle system process' and 'regulation of muscle system process' were enriched in the downregulated genes in dystrophic myoblasts.
source: Two broad GO categories: 'muscle system process' and 'regulation of muscle system process' were enriched in the downregulated genes found when comparing Dmdmdx and Dmdmdx-βgeo vs. WT primary mouse myoblasts (Figure 4a, Supplementary file 1-2).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: GO categories such as 'chromatin assembly' and 'muscle cell proliferation' are enriched in downregulated genes in dystrophic myoblasts, indicating an altered proliferative state.
source: Specifically, categories such as 'chromatin assembly' and 'muscle cell proliferation' (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 1-3), are enriched, indicating an altered proliferative state of dystrophic myoblasts.
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The enrichment of GO categories 'muscle cell migration' and 'positive regulation of cell migration' in downregulated genes indicate a migrative phenotype in dystrophic myoblasts.
source: The enrichment of the GO categories 'muscle cell migration' and 'positive regulation of cell migration' in downregulated genes (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1-3) indicate a migrative phenotype in dystrophic myoblasts, while GO categories 'muscle cell differentiation' and 'striated muscle cell differentiation' (Figure 4a and b- Supplementary files 1-3) suggest that dystrophic myoblasts may have an altered ability to differentiate.
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: GO categories 'muscle cell differentiation' and 'striated muscle cell differentiation' suggest that dystrophic myoblasts may have an altered ability to differentiate.
source: The enrichment of the GO categories 'muscle cell migration' and 'positive regulation of cell migration' in downregulated genes (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1-3) indicate a migrative phenotype in dystrophic myoblasts, while GO categories 'muscle cell differentiation' and 'striated muscle cell differentiation' (Figure 4a and b- Supplementary files 1-3) suggest that dystrophic myoblasts may have an altered ability to differentiate.
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Several GO categories related to calcium ion transport, homeostasis and calcium-mediated signalling were found significantly enriched in Dmdmdx vs. WT downregulated genes.
source: Moreover, several GO categories related to calcium ion transport, homeostasis and calcium-mediated signalling were found significantly enriched in Dmdmdx vs. WT downregulated genes (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 1-3), in line with this well-established dystrophic abnormality (Vallejo-Illarramendi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4b and citation to Vallejo-Illarramendi et al., 2014.

claim: After six hours of BrDU exposure, 57% of Dmdmdx myoblasts have incorporated BrDU compared to 26% of WT cells (p=3.0e-3).
source: After six hours, 57% of Dmdmdx myoblasts have incorporated BrDU compared to 26% of WT cells (p=3.0e-3). 39.1% of Dmdmdx-βgeo cells were positive for BrDU compared to 24% of the corresponding C57Bl/6 controls (p=1.0e-2).
evidence: This is based on BrDU incorporation assay data.

claim: 39.1% of Dmdmdx-βgeo cells were positive for BrDU compared to 24% of the corresponding C57Bl/6 controls (p=1.0e-2).
source: After six hours, 57% of Dmdmdx myoblasts have incorporated BrDU compared to 26% of WT cells (p=3.0e-3). 39.1% of Dmdmdx-βgeo cells were positive for BrDU compared to 24% of the corresponding C57Bl/6 controls (p=1.0e-2).
evidence: This is based on BrDU incorporation assay data.

claim: There is a statistically significant two-fold increase in BrDU incorporation denoting an exaggerated response to a proliferative stimulus in both dystrophic cells compared to their respective WT controls.
source: This statistically significant two-fold increase in BrDU incorporation denotes an exaggerated response to a proliferative stimulus in both dystrophic cells compared to their respective WT controls.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the BrDU incorporation assay data.

claim: Dp71 expression was described as enhancing myoblast proliferation.
source: Although Dp71 expression was described as enhancing myoblast proliferation (Farea et al., 2020), we did not observe any negative effect on proliferation in dystrophin-null Dmdmdx-βgeo cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Farea et al., 2020.

claim: No negative effect on proliferation was observed in dystrophin-null Dmdmdx-βgeo cells.
source: Although Dp71 expression was described as enhancing myoblast proliferation (Farea et al., 2020), we did not observe any negative effect on proliferation in dystrophin-null Dmdmdx-βgeo cells.
evidence: This is based on BrDU incorporation assay data comparing Dmdmdx-βgeo to controls.

source: Ultimately, myoblasts are the effector cells of muscle growth and repair, and it is the failure of muscle regeneration that drives DMD progression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about muscle biology.

source: Ultimately, myoblasts are the effector cells of muscle growth and repair, and it is the failure of muscle regeneration that drives DMD progression.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the role of myoblasts and the findings of this study.

source: These defects are cell autonomous rather than caused by the inflammatory environment of the dystrophic niche because they persist in the dystrophic cell line maintained long-term in culture: established cells reproduced the key transcriptomic anomalies and were described before to have functional alterations found in primary cells (Róg et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on comparison of primary cells and cell lines, with citation to Róg et al., 2019.

claim: Alterations in dystrophic myoblasts are shared between mouse and human DMD myoblasts, despite the significant heterogeneity within human samples.

evidence: This is based on cross-species comparison of RNA-Seq data.

claim: Dystrophic anomalies in myoblasts manifest irrespective of genetic backgrounds and across species, which confirms their significance.
source: Therefore, these dystrophic anomalies manifest irrespective of genetic backgrounds and across species, which confirms their significance.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cross-species and cross-genotype consistency of findings.

claim: Altered proliferation, migration and differentiation in DMD myoblasts have been reported.
source: Furthermore, altered proliferation, migration and differentiation in DMD myoblasts have been reported (Witkowski and Dubowitz, 1985; Melone et al., 2000; Nesmith et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2020) and our data provide the molecular underpinning for these abnormalities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Witkowski and Dubowitz, 1985; Melone et al., 2000; Nesmith et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2020.

claim: The data in this study provide the molecular underpinning for previously reported abnormalities in proliferation, migration and differentiation of DMD myoblasts.
source: Furthermore, altered proliferation, migration and differentiation in DMD myoblasts have been reported (Witkowski and Dubowitz, 1985; Melone et al., 2000; Nesmith et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2020) and our data provide the molecular underpinning for these abnormalities.
evidence: This is based on the transcriptomic and functional data presented in this study.

claim: There has been growing evidence that DMD mutations cause a range of cell-autonomous abnormalities in human and mouse myogenic cells and myoblasts, which affect cell division, differentiation, energy metabolism and signalling.
source: DMD pathology being intrinsic to the myoblast has been proposed previously (Blau et al., 1983) and there has been growing evidence that DMD mutations cause a range of cell-autonomous abnormalities in human and mouse myogenic cells and myoblasts, which affect cell division, differentiation, energy metabolism and signalling (Yablonka-Reuveni and Anderson, 2006; Yeung et al., 2006; Sacco et al., 2010; Sacco et al., 2010; Young et al., 2020; Young et al., 2020; Dumont et al., 2015b; Onopiuk et al., 2009; Onopiuk et al., 2015; Dumont et al., 2015a; Young et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting cell-autonomous abnormalities in myogenic cells.

claim: Altered proliferation and migration resulting in highly metastatic phenotypes have been associated with the loss of Dp427 in tumours featuring myogenic differentiation.
source: In fact, altered proliferation and migration resulting in highly metastatic phenotypes, have been associated with the loss of Dp427 in tumours featuring myogenic differentiation (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: DMD mutations evoke marked transcriptome and miRNome dysregulations early in human muscle cell development.
source: Our team recently demonstrated that DMD mutations evoke marked transcriptome and miRNome dysregulations early in human muscle cell development (Mournetas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mournetas et al., 2021.

claim: In a previous study, expression of key coordinators of muscle differentiation was dysregulated in proliferating dystrophic myoblasts, and differentiation was subsequently found to be altered.
source: In that study, expression of key coordinators of muscle differentiation was dysregulated in proliferating dystrophic myoblasts, the differentiation of which was subsequently also found to be altered, in line with the mouse cells studied here (Figure 5c).
evidence: This refers to findings from Mournetas et al., 2021 that are consistent with the current study.

claim: A significant number of downregulated transcripts in dystrophic myoblasts are controlled by the same TFs, most notably MyoD and MYOG.
source: A significant number of downregulated transcripts in dystrophic myoblasts are controlled by the same TFs, most notably MyoD and MYOG.
evidence: This is based on transcription factor binding site analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: The significant downregulation of Myod1 expression appears to be the key trigger mechanism of the dystrophic abnormality in myoblasts.
source: Given that MYOG itself is regulated by MyoD, the significant downregulation of Myod1 expression found here appears to be the key trigger mechanism of the dystrophic abnormality in myoblasts: the lower levels of Myod1 transcript strongly correlate with downregulated expression of genes controlled by this TF, and which are key coordinators of skeletal muscle repair.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of gene expression changes and known regulatory relationships.

claim: Complete Myod1 ablation in Dmdmdx has been shown to exacerbate the disease due to a diminished capability for muscle regeneration.
source: Indeed, complete Myod1 ablation in Dmdmdx has been shown to exacerbate the disease due to a diminished capability for muscle regeneration (Megeney et al., 1999; Schuierer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Megeney et al., 1999 and Schuierer et al., 2005.

claim: Downregulation of MyoD, which inhibits the cell cycle, could explain the increased proliferation in dystrophic cells.
source: Downregulation of MyoD, which inhibits the cell cycle, could explain the increased proliferation in dystrophic cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known function of MyoD and observed phenotype.

claim: The Myod1-Mymk-Mymx (Myomaker/ Myomixer) axis altered in dystrophic myoblasts was found to determine myotube formation.
source: The Myod1-Mymk-Mymx (Myomaker/ Myomixer) axis altered here was found to determine myotube formation (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Pax3 inhibits myogenic differentiation of myoblasts.
source: Given that Pax3 inhibits myogenic differentiation of myoblasts (Epstein et al., 1995), its downregulation in dystrophic cells could also contribute to this accelerated differentiation pattern observed here.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Epstein et al., 1995.

claim: Downregulation of Pax3 in dystrophic cells could contribute to the accelerated differentiation pattern observed.
source: Given that Pax3 inhibits myogenic differentiation of myoblasts (Epstein et al., 1995), its downregulation in dystrophic cells could also contribute to this accelerated differentiation pattern observed here.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known function of Pax3 and observed phenotype.

claim: Calsequestrins 1 and 2 levels being significantly downregulated is in line with previous findings in the dystrophic muscle and cell lines.
source: GO categories concerning calcium homeostasis and signalling, known to be altered in dystrophic muscles across species, were also found altered in dystrophic myoblasts: calsequestrins 1 and 2 levels being significantly downregulated, in line with previous findings in the dystrophic muscle Waugh et al., 2014; Doran et al., 2004 and cell lines (Róg et al., 2019; Onopiuk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Waugh et al., 2014; Doran et al., 2004; Róg et al., 2019; Onopiuk et al., 2015.

claim: In development, shorter dystrophins have been associated with proliferation and migration, and long isoforms with terminal commitment.
source: Given that Dp71 dystrophin is found in undifferentiated myogenic cells (Howard et al., 1999), and that in development shorter dystrophins have been associated with proliferation and migration, and long isoforms with terminal commitment (Hildyard et al., 2020), we hypothesized that eliminating expression of Dp71 may exacerbate dysfunctions in myogenic cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hildyard et al., 2020.

claim: Both Dmdmdx and Dmdmdx-βgeo cells had similar abnormalities.
source: Surprisingly, we found that both Dmdmdx and Dmdmdx-βgeo cells had similar abnormalities and, contrary to Dp71 overexpression increasing myoblast proliferation (Farea et al., 2020), BrdU incorporation in dystrophin-null myoblasts was still significantly increased compared to WT.
evidence: This is based on comparison of functional assays between the two dystrophic genotypes.

claim: Dmdmdx myoblasts, having a point mutation in exon 23, expressed significantly lower levels of Dp71.
source: Interestingly, Dmdmdx myoblasts, having a point mutation in exon 23, expressed significantly lower levels of Dp71 (Appendix 1—figure 1), whose expression is driven by a promoted located over 40 exons downstream of the mutation.
evidence: This is based on data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The data bring to light the significance of full-length dystrophin defects in undifferentiated muscle cells, the consequences of which correspond to the impaired muscle regeneration occurring in this disease.
source: Combined, these data bring to light the significance of full-length dystrophin defects in undifferentiated muscle cells, the consequences of which correspond to the impaired muscle regeneration occurring in this disease.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings.

claim: Dp427 in satellite cells appears to control asymmetrical cell division.
source: Dp427 in satellite cells appears to control asymmetrical cell division (Dumont et al., 2015b), which might suggest an interaction problem also in myoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dumont et al., 2015b.

claim: Even healthy myoblasts do not express Dp427 protein at levels detectable by Western blotting.
